prompt: In the rsyslog rule `auth,authpriv.*  /var/log/auth.log`, what does `.*` mean?

choices.text: Every severity
choices.why: Right. The part after the dot is the severity, and * takes all of them.

choices.text: Every user's messages
choices.why: rsyslog does not select by user.

choices.text: Every file under /var/log
choices.why: The destination is the right-hand side of the rule.

choices.text: Every program on the machine
choices.why: Programs are not in the selector; the facility before the dot groups them.

prompt: What is the effect of the `-` in `-/var/log/syslog`?

choices.text: Messages matching the rule are discarded instead of written to that file
choices.why: Discarding is written with `stop` or `~`; this writes them.

choices.text: The file is excluded from rotation, so it keeps growing until somebody empties it by hand
choices.why: Rotation is logrotate's business, in lesson 3.

choices.text: The file is written in binary, like the journal, and only journalctl reads it
choices.why: It is a text file; the journal is the binary one.

choices.text: rsyslog does not force each line to disk, so a crash loses the last few
choices.why: Right. Faster writes, and the most recent lines are the ones at risk.

prompt: ana runs `tail /var/log/auth.log` and gets `Permission denied`. What would let her read it, on Ubuntu, without becoming root?
hint: Look at the owner and group of the file.

choices.text: Reading /var/log/syslog instead
choices.why: It has the same owner, group and mode.

choices.text: Running `logger` first
choices.why: Writing a line does not grant reading the file.

choices.text: Membership of the adm group
choices.why: Right. The files are syslog:adm with mode rw-r-----.

choices.text: Membership of the syslog group
choices.why: syslog is the owner user; the group with read access is adm.

prompt: Match each message to the file rsyslog's default Ubuntu rules write it to.
hint: auth goes to one place, kern to another, the rest to a third.

prompt: In RFC 5424, which number is the severity `err`?
On Ubuntu 24.04, which program receives a message from sshd first?
hint: One of them writes text files from a copy.

choices.text: rsyslog
choices.why: It writes auth.log, but from what journald hands it.

choices.text: logrotate
choices.why: It rotates files on a schedule; it never receives messages.

choices.text: journald
choices.why: Right. rsyslog gets a copy from journald and writes the text files.

choices.text: auditd
choices.why: It records kernel audit events, a separate trail, and only when installed.

prompt: A minimal server has no /var/log/journal directory. It reboots after a crash. What happened to the journal from before the reboot?
hint: Where does journald keep it when that directory is missing?

choices.text: It is compressed into /var/log/journal.gz on shutdown
choices.why: There is no such file.

choices.text: It is intact under /var/log/journal, which journald creates as it starts
choices.why: journald uses that directory if it exists; it does not create it on its own.

choices.text: It was copied to /var/log/syslog before the reboot
choices.why: Only if rsyslog was running and received copies; the journal itself is still lost.

choices.text: It is gone: without that directory journald kept it in /run/log/journal, in memory
choices.why: Right. Volatile storage lasts until the next boot.

prompt: Which journalctl option filters by the systemd unit a message came from?

choices.text: -p
choices.why: -p filters by severity.

choices.text: -o
choices.why: -o chooses the output format.

choices.text: -u
choices.why: Right. `journalctl -u ssh.service`.

choices.text: -b
choices.why: -b limits to a boot.

prompt: An analyst looks for event 4688 on a fresh Windows installation and finds none, though programs clearly ran. Why?
hint: The Security channel writes only what something asks for.

choices.text: Event Viewer hides process events unless Sysmon is installed
choices.why: Sysmon adds its own channel; it does not unhide Security events.

choices.text: 4688 is written to the System channel rather than Security, so she was looking in the wrong place
choices.why: It is a Security event.

choices.text: Process creation is not enabled in the audit policy by default
choices.why: Right. auditpol has to turn it on; until then nothing is written.

choices.text: The events were overwritten because the channel was full
choices.why: Possible on a busy machine, but a fresh one with none at all points at the policy.

prompt: Two analysts, in São Paulo and in Lisbon, open the same 4625 event in Event Viewer and see different times. What is true?

choices.text: One of the two computers has a clock that is wrong
choices.why: Clock drift changes what is written, not how a stored time is displayed.

choices.text: The event holds one UTC time, shown in each viewer's local zone
choices.why: Right. Same instant, two displays.

choices.text: Event Viewer rounds times to the nearest hour for remote logs
choices.why: It does not round.

choices.text: Each copy of the event was written by a different domain controller
choices.why: It is the same event, read twice.

prompt: Match each Windows event id to what it records.
hint: 46xx is logons, 47xx accounts, 1102 the log itself.

prompt: A domain controller records 300 events 4625 in ten minutes, from one address, each for a different user name and each with status 0xC0000064. What is the most likely reading?
hint: What does 0xC0000064 say about the account?

choices.text: Three hundred accounts were locked out
choices.why: Lockouts are 4740, and accounts that do not exist cannot be locked.

choices.text: The domain controller's audit log was cleared
choices.why: That is 1102.

choices.text: Somebody is trying names that do not exist on the domain
choices.why: Right. 0xC0000064 is an account that does not exist; many names from one source is guessing names.

choices.text: One user keeps typing a wrong password
choices.why: That would be one name and 0xC000006A, the wrong password for an account that exists.

prompt: In an event 4624, which logon type means the session came through Remote Desktop?
Why is event 1102 useful even though it records the destruction of evidence?

choices.text: It prevents the log from being cleared again for a day
choices.why: Nothing in it blocks anything.

choices.text: It contains a backup of the events that were cleared
choices.why: It holds who cleared it, not the events.

choices.text: It is written after the clear, so the fact of the clearing survives it
choices.why: Right. The evidence is gone, and a record that it was removed remains, with who and when.

choices.text: Windows writes it to every other channel at the same time
choices.why: It is a Security event.

prompt: Match each Windows event to its closest Linux counterpart.
hint: Most of them live in auth.log.

prompt: `date -d 'Sep 17 02:33:07'` printed `Thu Sep 17 02:33:07 -03 2026`. Where did the year and the zone come from?

choices.text: From the machine where date ran
choices.why: Right. A record without them is read in the reader's year and zone.

choices.text: From the firewall that wrote the line
choices.why: The line carries no year and no zone to take them from.

choices.text: From the syslog standard, which fixes UTC-3
choices.why: No standard fixes a zone.

choices.text: From an NTP server
choices.why: NTP sets the clock; it does not annotate old lines.

prompt: An event is stamped 2026-09-17T23:10:00-03:00. What hour is it in UTC, on the 24-hour clock? Give the hour only.
hint: Add three hours, and mind the day.

prompt: gw's clock is 40 seconds fast and files' clock is right. gw logs a login at 02:33:47; files logs the copy it caused at 02:33:20. What does a timeline built from the raw stamps say?
hint: Correct one of them by 40 seconds and compare.

choices.text: The correct order, since 40 seconds is within normal tolerance
choices.why: The order flips, so the tolerance is not the issue.

choices.text: That the login and the copy happened in the same second
choices.why: They are 27 seconds apart as stamped.

choices.text: Nothing, because the two machines cannot be compared
choices.why: They can, once the drift is known; that is what NTP prevents having to do.

choices.text: That the copy happened before the login that caused it
choices.why: Right. Corrected, the login was at 02:33:07, before the copy; uncorrected, the order is reversed.

prompt: Order the life of an sshd message on Ubuntu 24.04, from the program to the file an analyst greps.
items: journald stores it with its fields
rsyslog receives a copy and matches auth,authpriv.*

prompt: You need to know when a package was installed on an Ubuntu server two months ago. Where do you look first?

choices.text: /var/log/wtmp
choices.why: wtmp records logins.

choices.text: /var/log/auth.log
choices.why: It holds logins and sudo; the sudo line is there, but not what apt did.

choices.text: /var/log/apt/history.log and its rotated copies
choices.why: Right. apt writes every install and removal there, with dates.

choices.text: /var/log/kern.log, where the kernel notes the modules and software it loads
choices.why: The kernel does not record package installs.

prompt: Somebody asks whether PowerShell code ran on a workstation last night, and what it said. Which channel answers, if it was enabled?

choices.text: Security
choices.why: 4688 there would show the process, not the script's text.

choices.text: Application
choices.why: Programs write there; PowerShell's script blocks go to their own channel.

choices.text: System
choices.why: System holds services and drivers.

choices.text: Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational
choices.why: Right. Script block logging writes 4104 there, with the code.
